topics.name: Introduction
topics.description: Terraform is a powerful tool designed by HashiCorp that helps you set up, manage, and update infrastructure safely and efficiently across various cloud providers. Think of it as a way to define your cloud resources—like servers, storage, and networks—using a simple code format. This makes it easier to automate, share, and manage your infrastructure, ensuring that everything is consistent and can be quickly reproduced or modified as needed.

resources.title: Terraform Backend: How it Works and How to Configure it

subtopics.name: What is Infrastructure as Code?
subtopics.description: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is a practice in DevOps and cloud computing that involves managing and provisioning computing infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files, rather than through physical hardware configuration or interactive configuration tools. This approach allows for version control, automation, and consistency in infrastructure deployment, making it easier to manage, scale, and replicate environments while reducing the risk of human error.

resources.title: What Is It? Why Is It Important?

subtopics.name: What is Terraform?
subtopics.description: Terraform is a powerful tool designed by HashiCorp that helps you set up, manage, and update infrastructure safely and efficiently across various cloud providers. Think of it as a way to define your cloud resources—like servers, storage, and networks—using a simple code format. This makes it easier to automate, share, and manage your infrastructure, ensuring that everything is consistent and can be quickly reproduced or modified as needed.

resources.title: What is Terraform? Terraform Explained in 2 Minutes

subtopics.name: Usecases and Benefits
subtopics.description: Terraform is used to automate the provisioning of cloud resources, manage multi-cloud environments from a single workflow, and enforce consistent infrastructure configurations across teams. Key benefits include reproducibility, reduced human error, faster deployments, and a full audit trail of infrastructure changes through version control.

resources.title: 9 Terraform Use Cases for Your Infrastructure as Code
What are the Benefits of Using Terraform?

subtopics.name: CaC vs IaC
subtopics.description: Configuration as Code (CaC) refers to managing the configuration of existing systems, such as installing software or setting up services on a server. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) refers to provisioning the underlying infrastructure itself, like virtual machines, networks, and storage. Terraform is an IaC tool; tools like Ansible or Chef are typically used for CaC, though there is overlap in practice.

resources.title: Ansible vs. Terraform: What's the difference?

subtopics.name: Installing Terraform
subtopics.description: To install Terraform, you need to download the appropriate package for your operating system from the official Terraform website. After downloading, unzip the package and move the executable to a directory included in your system's PATH. This allows you to run Terraform commands from the terminal. For more detailed installation instructions, refer to the links below.

topics.name: Hashicorp Config. Language (HCL)
topics.description: HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL) is a configuration language built by HashiCorp that is used for configuring products in the HashiCorp ecosystem. With its human-readable style, HCL is designed to strike a balance between a generic configuration language like JSON or YAML and a high-level scripting language. In relation to the Terraform Roadmap, HCL is the primary language used for writing Terraform configuration files, thus making it a fundamental part of defining and providing data center infrastructure in a descriptive manner.

subtopics.name: What is HCL?
subtopics.description: HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) is a structured configuration language designed to be easy for people to read and write. Terraform uses HCL in `.tf` files to describe infrastructure through blocks, arguments, and expressions. Terraform configurations are declarative: they describe the desired infrastructure state rather than a sequence of commands to create it.

subtopics.name: Basic Syntax
subtopics.description: The Basic Syntax of HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL) includes defining blocks, attributes, and expressions. Blocks are fundamental units like `resource`, `module`, and `provider`, identified by keywords and enclosed in curly braces. Attributes are key-value pairs within blocks, where keys are strings and values can be strings, numbers, or other data types. Expressions allow embedding variables, functions, and references to other resources, enabling dynamic configurations.

topics.name: Providers
topics.description: Terraform Providers are plugins that enable interaction with various external APIs. They manage the lifecycle of resources by defining resource types and data sources. Each provider requires configuration, typically including authentication details and endpoint URLs. Providers are specified in the `provider` block, and multiple providers can be used in a single Terraform project to manage resources across different platforms.

resources.title: What are terraform providers and how to use them?

subtopics.name: Terraform Registry
subtopics.description: The Terraform Registry is a centralized repository for discovering, sharing, and using Terraform modules and providers. It allows users to browse and download pre-built configurations, enabling quick integration of best practices. The registry supports versioning, ensuring consistent deployments, and includes detailed documentation for each module and provider. Users can also publish their own modules to the registry, facilitating community collaboration and reuse.

subtopics.name: Configuring Providers
subtopics.description: Configuring providers in Terraform involves specifying the required provider in the `provider` block within your Terraform configuration files. This block includes settings such as authentication credentials, region, and other provider-specific parameters. Providers must be initialized using `terraform init` to download and install the necessary plugins. Multiple configurations can be managed by aliasing providers, enabling resource management across different environments or accounts within the same provider.

subtopics.name: Versions
subtopics.description: Specifying provider versions in Terraform ensures consistent and predictable behavior across different environments. Instead of using the `version` meta-argument within the provider block, which was deprecated and removed in Terraform 0.13, provider version constraints should now be defined in the `required_providers` block. This approach prevents unexpected changes or compatibility issues due to provider updates, enhancing stability and reliability in infrastructure management. It allows you to control when and how provider updates are applied, ensuring that your infrastructure code runs with the expected provider functionality.

topics.name: Project Initialization
topics.description: Project initialization in Terraform involves setting up the necessary configuration files and directory structure for managing infrastructure as code. The `terraform init` command is crucial in this process, as it initializes the working directory, downloads the required provider plugins, and sets up the backend configuration for storing state files. This command ensures that the project is correctly configured and ready for subsequent Terraform commands, laying the foundation for efficient and organized infrastructure management.

subtopics.name: Input Variables
subtopics.description: Terraform input variables are parameters for modules, declared using variable blocks. They support multiple data types, default values, and descriptions. Users provide values when invoking modules or running Terraform. Accessed via `var.<name>` syntax, input variables enable flexible, reusable infrastructure templates adaptable to various deployment scenarios. They can be marked sensitive for security and are typically defined in a `variables.tf` file.

resources.title: Terraform Input and Output Variables Explained

topics.name: Resources
topics.description: Resources represent components of your infrastructure such as Virtual Machines, Storage Buckets, Databases or Virtual Private Clouds. Access to provider resources comes after successful project initialization after declaring your desired providers.

subtopics.name: Resource Behavior
subtopics.description: When Terraform applies a configuration, it determines what actions to take for each resource based on the difference between the desired state and the current state. Resources can be created, updated in place, destroyed and recreated, or left unchanged depending on what changed in the configuration. Some attributes require replacement rather than an in-place update.

resources.title: Terraform Resource Syntax, Behavior and State

subtopics.name: Resource Lifecycle
subtopics.description: The lifecycle meta-argument controls how Terraform manages a resource across plan and apply operations. Common settings include `create_before_destroy`, which ensures a replacement resource is created before the old one is removed, `prevent_destroy`, which blocks accidental deletion, and `ignore_changes`, which tells Terraform to ignore drift on specific attributes.

subtopics.name: Meta Arguments
subtopics.description: Meta-arguments are special arguments available on any resource block that change how Terraform handles that resource. They are not specific to a provider and are built into Terraform itself. Meta-arguments include `depends_on`, `count`, `for_each`, `provider`, and `lifecycle`.

subtopics.name: depends_on
subtopics.description: The depends\_on meta-argument in Terraform is used to explicitly declare dependencies between resources, ensuring that one or more resources are created or destroyed only after the specified dependent resources have been successfully applied. This is crucial for managing resource dependencies that are not automatically detected by Terraform’s implicit dependency analysis. By using depends\_on, you can enforce the correct order of resource creation, modification, or destruction, which is particularly useful in complex infrastructure setups where certain resources must exist or be configured before others can be effectively managed. This meta-argument enhances the reliability and predictability of your Terraform configurations

resources.title: How to use Terraform depends_on meta tag?

subtopics.name: Sensitive Data
subtopics.description: Terraform state may contain sensitive data such as passwords, private keys, and tokens returned by provider APIs. State files should be stored securely, with access restricted to authorized users and systems. Remote backends with encryption at rest and access controls are strongly recommended for any production use.

subtopics.name: Versioning
subtopics.description: State files can be versioned using backends that support versioning, such as S3 with versioning enabled. Keeping a history of state versions allows you to roll back to a previous state if a bad apply corrupts or loses data. Terraform Cloud and Enterprise provide built-in state history and the ability to restore past versions.

topics.name: Outputs
topics.description: Terraform outputs expose selected values from a configuration or module, making them accessible to users or other modules. Defined in output blocks, typically in an `outputs.tf` file, they can reference resource attributes or other computed values. Outputs are displayed after apply operations, can be queried using terraform output commands, and are crucial for passing information between modules or to external systems.

subtopics.name: Preconditions
subtopics.description: Terraform preconditions are declarative checks within resource or data blocks that validate configuration or state before Terraform attempts to create or modify resources. They use condition arguments to specify logical tests and `error_message` arguments for custom failure notifications. Preconditions help catch misconfigurations early, enforce business rules, and ensure dependencies are met before resource operations.

resources.title: Using Precondition and Post-condition Blocks in Terraform

topics.name: Variables
topics.description: Terraform uses variables to make configurations more flexible and reusable. Variables can be declared in `.tf` files and assigned values through various methods, including default values, command-line flags, environment variables, or separate `.tfvars` files. They support multiple data types such as string, number, bool, list, and map. Variables can be referenced throughout the configuration using the `var` prefix. This system enables infrastructure as code to be more dynamic and adaptable to different environments or use cases.

resources.title: Learn How to Use Terraform Variable

subtopics.name: Type Constraints
subtopics.description: Terraform variable type constraints specify allowed data types for input variables. They include primitive types (string, number, bool), complex types (list, set, map, object), and any for unspecified types. Constraints can enforce specific structures, nested types, or value ranges. They're defined in the variable block's type argument, helping catch errors early and ensuring correct variable usage throughout configurations.

subtopics.name: Variable Definition File
subtopics.description: A Terraform `variables.tf` file centralizes input variable declarations for a module or configuration. It typically contains multiple variable blocks, each defining a single input variable with its name, type constraint, optional default value, and description. This file serves as a single reference point for all variables used in the configuration, enhancing readability and maintainability. While not mandatory, using `variables.tf` is a common practice to organize and document a module's expected inputs.

resources.title: You should be using tfvars vs variables in Terraform

subtopics.name: Local Values
subtopics.description: Local values can be understood as a name assigned to any expression to use it multiple times directly by the name in your terraform module. Local values are referred to as locals and can be declared using the `locals` block. Local values can be a literal constants, resource attributes, variables, or other local values. Local values are helpful to define expressions or values that you need to use multiple times in the module as it allows the value to be updated easily just by updating the local value. A local value can be accessed using the `local` argument like `local.<value_name>`.

subtopics.name: Environment Variables
subtopics.description: Environment variables can be used to customize various aspects of Terraform. You can set these variables to change the default behaviour of terraform such as increase verbosity, update log file path, set workspace, etc. Environment variables are optional and terraform does not need them by default.

subtopics.name: Validation Rules
subtopics.description: Validation rules can be used to specify custom validations to a variable. The motive of adding validation rules is to make the variable comply with the rules. The validation rules can be added using a `validation` block.

topics.name: Format & Validate
topics.description: Terraform provides built-in commands for formatting and validating configuration files before deployment. These commands help maintain consistent style and catch configuration errors early, before a plan or apply is attempted.

resources.title: Validate, format, lint, secure, and test Terraform IaC
Terraform Validate Command – Validate Configuration Locally

subtopics.name: terraform fmt
subtopics.description: `terraform fmt` rewrites Terraform configuration files to the canonical format and style defined by HashiCorp. It adjusts indentation, alignment, and spacing. Running it regularly, or as part of a pre-commit hook, keeps configurations consistent across a team.

resources.title: Using Terraform fmt Command to Format Your Terraform Code

subtopics.name: terraform validate
subtopics.description: The validate command helps you make sure your Terraform code is syntactically correct before you deploy. This helps you to prevent misconfiguration due to missing attributes or incorrect dependencies, saving time, improving efficiency, and reducing cost.

subtopics.name: TFLint
subtopics.description: TFLint is a Terraform linter that goes beyond the checks provided by `terraform validate`. It detects errors specific to provider APIs, such as invalid instance types or unsupported regions, and can enforce custom coding rules through plugins. It is commonly run in CI pipelines alongside `terraform validate`.

resources.title: What is TFLint and How to Lint Your Terraform Code

topics.name: Best Practices for State
topics.description: State should never be stored in version control, as it may contain sensitive values and is not designed for manual editing. Use a remote backend with locking and versioning enabled. Keep state files small by splitting large configurations into smaller modules with independent state, and run `terraform refresh` carefully as it overwrites state with live data.

resources.title: Managing Terraform State – Best Practices & Examples
Best Practices for Terraform State File Management
Managing Terraform State Files - What are your options?

subtopics.name: count
subtopics.description: The `count` meta-argument creates multiple instances of a resource or module from a single block. It accepts a whole number, and each instance is identified by an index starting at zero. Individual instances can be referenced using the `resource.name[index]` syntax.

resources.title: Conditional blocks in Terraform using count

subtopics.name: for_each
subtopics.description: The `for_each` meta-argument creates one instance of a resource or module for each item in a map or set of strings. Each instance is keyed by the map key or set value, making it easier to manage and reference individual items than with `count`. It is generally preferred over `count` when creating resources from a collection.

subtopics.name: provider
subtopics.description: The `provider` meta-argument assigns a specific provider configuration to a resource when multiple configurations of the same provider exist. This is common when managing resources across multiple regions or accounts within the same Terraform workspace. The value must match an alias defined in a `provider` block.

subtopics.name: lifecycle
subtopics.description: The `lifecycle` block inside a resource configures how Terraform handles creation, updates, and deletion of that resource. It supports arguments like `create_before_destroy`, `prevent_destroy`, `ignore_changes`, and `replace_triggered_by`. These settings give you fine-grained control over resource replacement behavior.

topics.name: State
topics.description: Terraform state is a file that records the current status of managed infrastructure. It maps resources in the configuration to real-world objects and stores attribute values returned by the provider after creation. State is used to compute diffs during planning and to track resource identity across operations.

subtopics.name: Splitting State Files
subtopics.description: Large Terraform configurations can be split into multiple state files by organizing resources into separate workspaces or root modules. This reduces the blast radius of plan and apply operations, speeds up plans, and makes it easier for teams to work independently on different parts of the infrastructure.

subtopics.name: Import Existing Resources
subtopics.description: `terraform import` brings existing infrastructure resources under Terraform management by adding them to the state file. After importing, the configuration must be written manually to match the imported resource. This is used when adopting Terraform in environments where resources were created outside of it.

resources.title: Terraform Import: What it is and how to use it
Exploring the Import Block in Terraform 1.5

subtopics.name: State Locking
subtopics.description: State locking prevents two Terraform operations from modifying state at the same time. When supported by the backend, Terraform acquires a lock before writing to state and releases it when the operation completes. If a lock is not released due to a crash or error, it can be manually removed with the `force-unlock` command.

subtopics.name: Remote State
subtopics.description: Remote state stores the Terraform state file in a shared, remote backend such as S3, Azure Blob Storage, or Terraform Cloud. This allows multiple team members to work with the same state and prevents conflicts from concurrent operations. Remote backends also support state locking to prevent simultaneous writes.

subtopics.name: Published Modules Usage
subtopics.description: Published modules are pre-built, versioned modules available on the Terraform Registry. They can be referenced directly in a `module` block using a registry source address and version constraint. Using published modules speeds up development by providing tested, maintained implementations of common infrastructure patterns.

subtopics.name: Creating Local Modules
subtopics.description: Local modules are directories containing Terraform configuration files that are referenced using a relative file path in a `module` block. They allow you to break a large configuration into smaller, self-contained units. Inputs are passed via variables and outputs are declared for the parent module to consume.

resources.title: Build and use a local module
How to create reusable infrastructure with Terraform modules

subtopics.name: Inputs / Outputs
subtopics.description: Modules accept input values through declared variables and expose results through declared outputs. The calling module passes values for each required variable and can reference the module's outputs using the `module.<name>.<output>` syntax. Well-defined inputs and outputs form the public interface of a module.

subtopics.name: Modules Best Practices
subtopics.description: Modules should be focused on a single concern and avoid hardcoding values that callers need to control. Always declare types for input variables and provide descriptions. Version-pin external modules and keep local modules small and composable. Avoid deeply nested module hierarchies, as they are harder to debug and maintain.

resources.title: Terraform Modules Guide: Best Practices & Examples
Best practices for modularizing a Terraform project | PlatformCon 2023

topics.name: Inspect / Modify State
topics.description: Terraform provides a set of commands for inspecting and modifying state directly. These are advanced operations used to fix drift, remove orphaned resources, or manually adjust state when normal plan and apply workflows are insufficient.

resources.title: How to Manage Terraform State: A Step-by-Step Guide

subtopics.name: Output Syntax
subtopics.description: An output block requires a `value` argument that specifies what to expose. Optional arguments include `description` for documentation, `sensitive` to redact the value, and `depends_on` to declare explicit dependencies. Outputs can expose any value, including resource attributes, local values, and variable values.

resources.title: Terraform Output Values : Complete Guide & Examples
Terraform: Output a field from a module

subtopics.name: Sensitive Outputs
subtopics.description: Marking an output as sensitive tells Terraform to redact its value from CLI output and logs. The value is still stored in state and can be accessed programmatically. This is commonly used for passwords, tokens, and other secrets that should not appear in plain text in terminal output.

resources.title: How to output sensitive data in Terraform

subtopics.name: graph
subtopics.description: `terraform graph` outputs a visual representation of the dependency graph for the current configuration or plan. The output is in DOT format, which can be rendered with tools like Graphviz. It is useful for understanding resource dependencies and diagnosing unexpected ordering issues.

resources.title: How to Generate Images with Terraform Graph Command

subtopics.name: show
subtopics.description: `terraform show` displays a human-readable representation of the current state or a saved plan file. It is useful for reviewing what Terraform currently knows about managed resources without running a full plan. Passing a plan file shows the exact changes that will be applied.

subtopics.name: list
subtopics.description: `terraform state list` prints the addresses of all resources tracked in the current state. It is a quick way to see what Terraform is managing and to find the exact resource address needed for other state subcommands. Addresses can be filtered by a resource type or module prefix.

subtopics.name: output
subtopics.description: `terraform output` displays the values of outputs defined in the configuration. Without arguments it shows all outputs; a specific output name can be passed to retrieve a single value. The `-json` flag returns output in machine-readable format, useful for scripting.

subtopics.name: rm
subtopics.description: `terraform state rm` removes one or more resources from the state file without destroying the actual infrastructure. This is used when you want Terraform to stop managing a resource, for example before importing it into a different workspace or before deleting it manually.

resources.title: Terraform State Rm: How to Remove a Resource From State File
How to remove resource from Terraform state file | terraform state rm example

subtopics.name: mv
subtopics.description: `terraform state mv` moves a resource address from one location to another within the state file. It is used when refactoring configurations, such as renaming a resource or moving it into a module, without triggering a destroy and recreate cycle.

subtopics.name: -replace option in apply
subtopics.description: The `-replace` flag on `terraform apply` forces Terraform to destroy and recreate a specific resource even if no configuration changes would normally trigger replacement. It is used to resolve issues with a corrupted or degraded resource that needs to be rebuilt. This replaces the older `taint` command.

resources.title: Terraform Taint, Untaint, Replace – How to Use It (Examples)
Terraform Taint Is Bad Actually - Use Replace Instead

subtopics.name: state pull / push
subtopics.description: `terraform state pull` downloads the current remote state and prints it to stdout. `terraform state push` uploads a local state file to the configured backend, overwriting the remote state. These commands are used for manual state recovery or migration and should be used with caution.

resources.title: Migrate Workspace State Using Terraform State Push / Pull

subtopics.name: state replace-provider
subtopics.description: `terraform state replace-provider` updates all resource entries in the state that reference one provider to reference a different provider. This is used when migrating resources to a forked or renamed provider without destroying and recreating them.

subtopics.name: state force-unlock
subtopics.description: `terraform state force-unlock` manually releases a state lock that was not properly released after an interrupted operation. It requires the lock ID, which is displayed in the error message shown when a lock conflict is detected. This command should only be used when you are certain no other Terraform operation is running.

topics.name: Clean Up
topics.description: Cleaning up Terraform-managed infrastructure means removing resources that are no longer needed. Terraform provides a command to destroy all resources in the current workspace, and understanding when and how to use it safely is an important part of the infrastructure lifecycle.

subtopics.name: terraform destroy
subtopics.description: `terraform destroy` removes all resources managed by the current configuration. It is the equivalent of running `terraform apply` with every resource marked for deletion. Like apply, it shows a plan and prompts for confirmation before proceeding. Individual resources can also be targeted with the `-target` flag.

topics.name: Deployment
topics.description: Deployment refers to the process of applying a configuration to create or update infrastructure. The typical workflow involves running `terraform plan` to preview changes and `terraform apply` to execute them. Understanding what happens during these steps is necessary for safe and predictable infrastructure management.

subtopics.name: terraform plan
subtopics.description: `terraform plan` computes the difference between the current state and the desired configuration and displays the actions Terraform would take. It does not make any changes to infrastructure. The plan can be saved to a file and passed to `terraform apply` to ensure the exact previewed changes are applied.

resources.title: Terraform plan command and how it works

subtopics.name: terraform apply
subtopics.description: `terraform apply` is the command used to implement the changes defined in your Terraform configuration files. It creates, updates, or deletes the specified infrastructure resources to match the desired state. Before making changes, it shows a plan similar to terraform plan and prompts for confirmation, unless the -auto-approve flag is used. Apply updates the state file to reflect the current infrastructure state, enabling Terraform to track and manage resources over time. It handles dependencies between resources, creating them in the correct order.

resources.title: Terraform Apply Command: Options, Examples and Best Practices

topics.name: Modules
topics.description: Modules are reusable packages of Terraform configuration that group related resources together. They allow you to abstract and share infrastructure patterns across projects and teams. Every Terraform configuration is technically a module; the directory you run Terraform from is called the root module.

subtopics.name: Root vs Child Modules
subtopics.description: The root module is the working directory where Terraform is invoked. Child modules are called from the root module or from other modules using a `module` block. Child modules can be local directories or remote sources such as the Terraform Registry or a Git repository.

resources.title: What is the difference between Terraform "Module" and "Child Module"

topics.name: Provisioners
topics.description: Provisioners run scripts or commands on local or remote machines as part of resource creation or destruction. They are a last resort for handling bootstrapping or configuration tasks that cannot be done through the provider API. HashiCorp recommends using purpose-built tools like cloud-init or Ansible instead where possible.

subtopics.name: When to Use?
subtopics.description: Provisioners are appropriate when no provider resource or data source can accomplish the required task and the action must happen at resource creation or destruction time. Common use cases include running initialization scripts on a new server or notifying an external system after a resource is created. They should be avoided when alternatives exist because they add complexity and are harder to test.

resources.title: Why You should Use Terraform Provisioners as a Final Option
Why Terraform Provisioners Are The Last Resort?

subtopics.name: Creation / Destroy Time
subtopics.description: Provisioners run either at creation time, after the resource is created, or at destroy time, before the resource is deleted. Creation-time provisioners bootstrap resources, while destroy-time provisioners handle cleanup tasks. If a creation-time provisioner fails, the resource is marked as tainted and will be destroyed and recreated on the next apply.

resources.title: How to: Terraform destroy time provisioners

subtopics.name: file provisioner
subtopics.description: The `file` provisioner copies files or directories from the machine running Terraform to a newly created remote resource. It requires a connection block specifying how to reach the remote machine, typically over SSH or WinRM. It is commonly used to upload configuration files or scripts before executing them.

subtopics.name: local-exec provisioner
subtopics.description: The `local-exec` provisioner runs a command on the machine executing Terraform, not on the remote resource. It is used for tasks like triggering an external API, running a local script, or writing data to a file. The command runs in a shell, and the working directory defaults to the Terraform configuration directory.

subtopics.name: remote-exec provisioner
subtopics.description: The `remote-exec` provisioner runs commands on the remote resource after it is created. It connects over SSH or WinRM and executes a list of inline commands or a script file. It is often used to install software or run configuration steps that cannot be handled by the provider.

subtopics.name: Custom Provisioners
subtopics.description: Custom provisioners can be implemented using external programs that follow the Terraform provisioner plugin protocol. They allow teams to integrate specialized tooling into the Terraform lifecycle without relying on the built-in provisioner types. Custom provisioners are rare and typically only needed for highly specific workflows.

resources.title: Terraform Provisioners - Why you should avoid them

topics.name: Data Sources
topics.description: Data sources allow Terraform to read information from external systems or from resources not managed in the current configuration. A `data` block queries a provider for information at plan time and makes the result available as a reference. Common uses include looking up AMI IDs, VPC details, or DNS zone information.

resources.title: Terraform Data Sources – How They Are Utilized

topics.name: Template Files
topics.description: Template files use the `templatefile` function to render a file with variable substitutions at plan time. The function takes a file path and a map of values and returns the rendered string. Template files are commonly used to generate user data scripts, configuration files, or policy documents from dynamic values.

topics.name: CI / CD Integration
topics.description: Integrating Terraform into a CI/CD pipeline automates infrastructure changes through the same review and deployment process used for application code. A typical pipeline runs `terraform fmt`, `terraform validate`, and `terraform plan` on pull requests, and `terraform apply` on merges to the main branch. Automation reduces human error and enforces a consistent workflow.

subtopics.name: GitHub Actions
subtopics.description: GitHub Actions can run Terraform commands as part of a workflow triggered by pull requests or pushes. Workflows are defined in YAML files and can use community actions from the GitHub Marketplace or call the Terraform CLI directly. Secrets for provider credentials are stored in the repository settings and injected as environment variables.

resources.title: Terraform with GitHub Actions : How to Manage & Scale

subtopics.name: Circle CI
subtopics.description: CircleCI can execute Terraform pipelines using orbs or custom job configurations. Jobs are defined in a `.circleci/config.yml` file and run in containers with the Terraform binary installed. It supports parallel jobs, caching, and approval steps that can be used to gate a `terraform apply` behind a manual review.

resources.title: Deploy Infrastructure with Terraform and CircleCI
How I deployed terraform resources with CircleCI

subtopics.name: GitLab CI
subtopics.description: GitLab CI runs Terraform pipelines using `.gitlab-ci.yml` configuration files. GitLab provides a native Terraform integration with merge request widgets that display plan output directly in the code review interface. The GitLab-managed Terraform state backend stores state securely within the GitLab instance.

resources.title: Infrastructure as Code with Terraform and GitLab
How to Implement GitLab CI/CD Pipeline with Terraform
Automate deploying to AWS using Terraform with GitLab CICD pipeline

subtopics.name: Jenkins
subtopics.description: Jenkins can orchestrate Terraform workflows using Pipeline scripts written in Groovy. The Terraform binary is installed on agents or provided via a tool configuration. Jenkins supports approval gates between plan and apply stages and integrates with secret management tools to supply provider credentials securely.

resources.title: Terraform with Jenkins – How to Manage Workflows
How to Use Terraform and Jenkins to Automate Infrastructure Setup

topics.name: Workspaces
topics.description: Workspaces allow multiple state files to exist for the same configuration, enabling the same code to manage separate environments such as development, staging, and production. The `terraform workspace` commands create, switch, and list workspaces. The current workspace name is available in expressions as `terraform.workspace`.

resources.title: Structuring Repositories for Terraform Workspaces - Hashicorp

topics.name: Scaling Terraform
topics.description: As infrastructure grows, Terraform configurations must be structured to remain manageable, performant, and safe for teams to use concurrently. Scaling strategies include splitting state, parallelizing operations, enforcing consistent deployment workflows, and managing version drift across modules and providers.

subtopics.name: Version Management
subtopics.description: Managing Terraform and provider versions across a team requires consistent tooling. `tfenv` is a popular version manager for Terraform that allows switching between installed versions based on a `.terraform-version` file. Pinning versions in `required_version` and `required_providers` blocks ensures everyone uses compatible releases.

resources.title: How to Use tfenv to Manage Multiple Terraform Versions

subtopics.name: Splitting Large State
subtopics.description: Large state files slow down plans and increase the risk of conflicts. Splitting infrastructure into smaller, independently managed configurations with their own state files reduces plan times and limits the impact of a failed apply. Resources in different state files communicate through remote state data sources or variable passing.

subtopics.name: Parallelism
subtopics.description: Terraform applies resource changes in parallel by default, up to a configurable limit controlled by the `-parallelism` flag. Increasing parallelism can speed up large deployments but may hit API rate limits. Lowering it can reduce throttling errors when working with providers that enforce strict rate limits.

resources.title: Considerations when setting the TFE_PARALLELISM environment variable

subtopics.name: Deployment Workflow
subtopics.description: A consistent deployment workflow defines how infrastructure changes move from development to production. Common patterns include environment promotion, where changes are applied to lower environments first, and GitOps, where the desired state is tracked in a Git repository and applied automatically. Enforcing a workflow reduces the risk of ad-hoc changes causing drift.

resources.title: Advanced Concepts and Faster Workflows in the Terraform Language

subtopics.name: Terragrunt
subtopics.description: Terragrunt is a thin wrapper around Terraform that adds support for keeping configurations DRY, managing dependencies between modules, and running commands across multiple modules at once. It uses `terragrunt.hcl` files to define module sources, variable inputs, and backend configuration. It is widely used in large multi-account or multi-environment Terraform setups.

resources.title: Terragrunt Tutorial: Examples and Use Cases

subtopics.name: Infracost
subtopics.description: Infracost is a cost estimation tool that integrates with Terraform to show the monthly cloud cost impact of planned infrastructure changes. It parses a Terraform plan and calculates costs based on provider pricing data. It can be added to CI pipelines to display cost breakdowns in pull request comments before changes are merged.

resources.title: Shifting FinOps Left: A live demo

topics.name: Testing
topics.description: Testing Terraform configurations verifies that infrastructure behaves as expected before and after deployment. Testing strategies range from static analysis and unit tests on modules to integration and end-to-end tests that provision real infrastructure. A layered testing approach catches different classes of problems at different stages of development.

subtopics.name: Unit Testing
subtopics.description: Unit tests for Terraform validate individual modules in isolation, checking that inputs produce the expected plan output without provisioning real resources. The native `terraform test` command introduced in Terraform 1.6 supports this by running configurations in a controlled context. Tools like Terratest can also be used for more complex scenarios.

subtopics.name: Contract Testing
subtopics.description: Contract testing verifies that the inputs and outputs of a module conform to a defined interface. It ensures that a module behaves predictably when called with specific values and that its outputs meet the expectations of callers. This is useful when modules are shared across multiple teams or projects.

resources.title: Contract Testing: An Introduction and Guide
Contract testing for microservices is a must!

subtopics.name: Integration Testing
subtopics.description: Integration tests provision real infrastructure and verify that resources are created correctly and work together as expected. They are slower and more expensive than unit tests but catch issues that static analysis cannot detect. Terratest is a popular Go-based framework for writing integration tests against live Terraform deployments.

resources.title: Learn Terraform - Integration and End-to-End Testing

subtopics.name: End to End Testing
subtopics.description: End-to-end tests validate an entire infrastructure stack by provisioning it, running checks against live endpoints or resources, and then tearing it down. These tests are the most comprehensive but also the slowest and most costly. They are typically run in a dedicated test environment and triggered on a schedule or before major releases.

resources.title: Getting Started: End to End Tests
End To End Testing On Terraform With Terratest

subtopics.name: Testing Modules
subtopics.description: Testing modules involves validating their logic, variable handling, and output values in isolation before they are used in a larger configuration. The `terraform test` command can apply a module with test-specific variable values and assert expected output values. Keeping modules testable means writing them with clear inputs and outputs and minimal side effects.

topics.name: Security
topics.description: Securing a Terraform workflow involves protecting secrets, enforcing policy on what infrastructure can be provisioned, and scanning configurations for misconfigurations before they reach production. A layered approach combines secret management, policy as code, and static analysis tools.

subtopics.name: Secret Management
subtopics.description: Secrets such as API keys, passwords, and certificates should never be stored in Terraform configuration files or committed to version control. Common approaches include injecting secrets via environment variables, using a secrets manager like HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager as a data source, or using a backend that encrypts sensitive state values.

resources.title: Terraform Secrets - How to manage them
A comprehensive guide to managing secrets in your Terraform code

subtopics.name: Compliance / Sentinel
subtopics.description: Sentinel is a policy as code framework built into Terraform Cloud and Enterprise. It allows teams to define rules that restrict what infrastructure can be provisioned, enforce tagging standards, or require cost approval before applying. Policies are evaluated between the plan and apply phases, blocking deployments that violate defined rules.

subtopics.name: Terrascan
subtopics.description: Terrascan is an open-source static analysis tool that scans Terraform configurations for security and compliance violations before deployment. It checks against a library of built-in policies covering common cloud security standards and supports custom rules. It can be integrated into CI pipelines to fail builds that introduce insecure configurations.

subtopics.name: Checkov
subtopics.description: Checkov is a static analysis tool for infrastructure as code that scans Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, and other formats for security and compliance issues. It includes hundreds of built-in checks covering major cloud providers and supports custom policies written in Python or YAML. Scan results can be output as JUnit XML for integration with CI systems.

subtopics.name: Trivy
subtopics.description: Trivy is a security scanner that can analyze Terraform configurations for misconfigurations in addition to scanning container images and filesystems. It checks infrastructure code against a set of built-in rules and reports issues by severity. Trivy is easy to integrate into CI workflows and supports multiple output formats.

resources.title: How to secure Terraform code with Trivy

subtopics.name: KICS
subtopics.description: KICS (Keeping Infrastructure as Code Secure) is an open-source tool from Checkmarx that scans IaC files including Terraform for security vulnerabilities, compliance issues, and misconfigurations. It covers a broad set of cloud platforms and IaC formats and supports custom queries written in the Open Policy Agent Rego language.

topics.name: HCP
topics.description: HCP (HashiCorp Cloud Platform) is a managed cloud offering that hosts HashiCorp products including Terraform as a service. It provides a centralized place to manage Terraform runs, state, and policies without self-hosting the Terraform Enterprise platform.

subtopics.name: What and when to use HCP?
subtopics.description: HCP Terraform is appropriate when a team wants the benefits of Terraform Cloud, such as remote runs, state management, and policy enforcement, without managing infrastructure for it. It suits teams that are scaling beyond local Terraform workflows and need collaboration features, audit logs, and a managed backend. It is available in free and paid tiers.

subtopics.name: Enterprise Features
subtopics.description: HCP Terraform Enterprise features include audit logging, single sign-on, self-hosted deployment options, Sentinel policy enforcement, team and organization management, and private module registries. These features are aimed at large organizations that need governance controls and compliance capabilities beyond what the free tier provides.

resources.title: How does The Infrastructure Cloud work?

subtopics.name: Authentication
subtopics.description: HCP Terraform authenticates users and services through API tokens. User tokens are generated in the account settings and used for CLI access. Service account tokens are used in CI/CD pipelines. The `terraform login` command stores credentials locally for CLI use.

subtopics.name: Workspaces
subtopics.description: HCP Terraform workspaces are managed environments that store state, run history, and variable values for a specific configuration. Each workspace is linked to a version control repository or configured for CLI-driven runs. Variables and sensitive values are stored per workspace and injected into runs automatically.

resources.title: Organize your Terraform Cloud workspaces using Projects

subtopics.name: VCS Integration
subtopics.description: HCP Terraform integrates with version control systems including GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps. Linking a workspace to a VCS repository triggers speculative plans on pull requests and applies on merges to the configured branch. This brings infrastructure changes into the same code review workflow as application changes.

resources.title: Connecting VCS Providers to HCP Terraform

subtopics.name: Run Tasks
subtopics.description: Run Tasks are integrations that execute external services at specific points in the Terraform run lifecycle, such as after a plan or before an apply. They can be used to trigger security scans, cost checks, or custom validation logic. Run tasks return a pass or fail result that can block or allow the apply from proceeding.

nodes.name: Introduction
nodes.description: Terraform is a powerful tool designed by HashiCorp that helps you set up, manage, and update infrastructure safely and efficiently across various cloud providers. Think of it as a way to define your cloud resources—like servers, storage, and networks—using a simple code format. This makes it easier to automate, share, and manage your infrastructure, ensuring that everything is consistent and can be quickly reproduced or modified as needed.

resources.title: Terraform Backend: How it Works and How to Configure it

nodes.name: What is Infrastructure as Code?
nodes.description: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is a practice in DevOps and cloud computing that involves managing and provisioning computing infrastructure through machine-readable configuration files, rather than through physical hardware configuration or interactive configuration tools. This approach allows for version control, automation, and consistency in infrastructure deployment, making it easier to manage, scale, and replicate environments while reducing the risk of human error.

resources.title: What Is It? Why Is It Important?

nodes.name: What is Terraform?
nodes.description: Terraform is a powerful tool designed by HashiCorp that helps you set up, manage, and update infrastructure safely and efficiently across various cloud providers. Think of it as a way to define your cloud resources—like servers, storage, and networks—using a simple code format. This makes it easier to automate, share, and manage your infrastructure, ensuring that everything is consistent and can be quickly reproduced or modified as needed.

resources.title: What is Terraform? Terraform Explained in 2 Minutes

nodes.name: Usecases and Benefits
nodes.description: Terraform is used to automate the provisioning of cloud resources, manage multi-cloud environments from a single workflow, and enforce consistent infrastructure configurations across teams. Key benefits include reproducibility, reduced human error, faster deployments, and a full audit trail of infrastructure changes through version control.

resources.title: 9 Terraform Use Cases for Your Infrastructure as Code
What are the Benefits of Using Terraform?

nodes.name: CaC vs IaC
nodes.description: Configuration as Code (CaC) refers to managing the configuration of existing systems, such as installing software or setting up services on a server. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) refers to provisioning the underlying infrastructure itself, like virtual machines, networks, and storage. Terraform is an IaC tool; tools like Ansible or Chef are typically used for CaC, though there is overlap in practice.

resources.title: Ansible vs. Terraform: What's the difference?

nodes.name: Installing Terraform
nodes.description: To install Terraform, you need to download the appropriate package for your operating system from the official Terraform website. After downloading, unzip the package and move the executable to a directory included in your system's PATH. This allows you to run Terraform commands from the terminal. For more detailed installation instructions, refer to the links below.

nodes.name: Hashicorp Config. Language (HCL)
nodes.description: HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL) is a configuration language built by HashiCorp that is used for configuring products in the HashiCorp ecosystem. With its human-readable style, HCL is designed to strike a balance between a generic configuration language like JSON or YAML and a high-level scripting language. In relation to the Terraform Roadmap, HCL is the primary language used for writing Terraform configuration files, thus making it a fundamental part of defining and providing data center infrastructure in a descriptive manner.

nodes.name: What is HCL?
nodes.description: HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) is a structured configuration language designed to be easy for people to read and write. Terraform uses HCL in `.tf` files to describe infrastructure through blocks, arguments, and expressions. Terraform configurations are declarative: they describe the desired infrastructure state rather than a sequence of commands to create it.

nodes.name: Basic Syntax
nodes.description: The Basic Syntax of HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL) includes defining blocks, attributes, and expressions. Blocks are fundamental units like `resource`, `module`, and `provider`, identified by keywords and enclosed in curly braces. Attributes are key-value pairs within blocks, where keys are strings and values can be strings, numbers, or other data types. Expressions allow embedding variables, functions, and references to other resources, enabling dynamic configurations.

nodes.name: Providers
nodes.description: Terraform Providers are plugins that enable interaction with various external APIs. They manage the lifecycle of resources by defining resource types and data sources. Each provider requires configuration, typically including authentication details and endpoint URLs. Providers are specified in the `provider` block, and multiple providers can be used in a single Terraform project to manage resources across different platforms.

resources.title: What are terraform providers and how to use them?

nodes.name: Terraform Registry
nodes.description: The Terraform Registry is a centralized repository for discovering, sharing, and using Terraform modules and providers. It allows users to browse and download pre-built configurations, enabling quick integration of best practices. The registry supports versioning, ensuring consistent deployments, and includes detailed documentation for each module and provider. Users can also publish their own modules to the registry, facilitating community collaboration and reuse.

nodes.name: Configuring Providers
nodes.description: Configuring providers in Terraform involves specifying the required provider in the `provider` block within your Terraform configuration files. This block includes settings such as authentication credentials, region, and other provider-specific parameters. Providers must be initialized using `terraform init` to download and install the necessary plugins. Multiple configurations can be managed by aliasing providers, enabling resource management across different environments or accounts within the same provider.

nodes.name: Versions
nodes.description: Specifying provider versions in Terraform ensures consistent and predictable behavior across different environments. Instead of using the `version` meta-argument within the provider block, which was deprecated and removed in Terraform 0.13, provider version constraints should now be defined in the `required_providers` block. This approach prevents unexpected changes or compatibility issues due to provider updates, enhancing stability and reliability in infrastructure management. It allows you to control when and how provider updates are applied, ensuring that your infrastructure code runs with the expected provider functionality.

nodes.name: Project Initialization
nodes.description: Project initialization in Terraform involves setting up the necessary configuration files and directory structure for managing infrastructure as code. The `terraform init` command is crucial in this process, as it initializes the working directory, downloads the required provider plugins, and sets up the backend configuration for storing state files. This command ensures that the project is correctly configured and ready for subsequent Terraform commands, laying the foundation for efficient and organized infrastructure management.

nodes.name: Input Variables
nodes.description: Terraform input variables are parameters for modules, declared using variable blocks. They support multiple data types, default values, and descriptions. Users provide values when invoking modules or running Terraform. Accessed via `var.<name>` syntax, input variables enable flexible, reusable infrastructure templates adaptable to various deployment scenarios. They can be marked sensitive for security and are typically defined in a `variables.tf` file.

resources.title: Terraform Input and Output Variables Explained

nodes.name: Resources
nodes.description: Resources represent components of your infrastructure such as Virtual Machines, Storage Buckets, Databases or Virtual Private Clouds. Access to provider resources comes after successful project initialization after declaring your desired providers.

nodes.name: Resource Behavior
nodes.description: When Terraform applies a configuration, it determines what actions to take for each resource based on the difference between the desired state and the current state. Resources can be created, updated in place, destroyed and recreated, or left unchanged depending on what changed in the configuration. Some attributes require replacement rather than an in-place update.

resources.title: Terraform Resource Syntax, Behavior and State

nodes.name: Resource Lifecycle
nodes.description: The lifecycle meta-argument controls how Terraform manages a resource across plan and apply operations. Common settings include `create_before_destroy`, which ensures a replacement resource is created before the old one is removed, `prevent_destroy`, which blocks accidental deletion, and `ignore_changes`, which tells Terraform to ignore drift on specific attributes.

nodes.name: Meta Arguments
nodes.description: Meta-arguments are special arguments available on any resource block that change how Terraform handles that resource. They are not specific to a provider and are built into Terraform itself. Meta-arguments include `depends_on`, `count`, `for_each`, `provider`, and `lifecycle`.

nodes.name: depends_on
nodes.description: The depends\_on meta-argument in Terraform is used to explicitly declare dependencies between resources, ensuring that one or more resources are created or destroyed only after the specified dependent resources have been successfully applied. This is crucial for managing resource dependencies that are not automatically detected by Terraform’s implicit dependency analysis. By using depends\_on, you can enforce the correct order of resource creation, modification, or destruction, which is particularly useful in complex infrastructure setups where certain resources must exist or be configured before others can be effectively managed. This meta-argument enhances the reliability and predictability of your Terraform configurations

resources.title: How to use Terraform depends_on meta tag?

nodes.name: Sensitive Data
nodes.description: Terraform state may contain sensitive data such as passwords, private keys, and tokens returned by provider APIs. State files should be stored securely, with access restricted to authorized users and systems. Remote backends with encryption at rest and access controls are strongly recommended for any production use.

nodes.name: Versioning
nodes.description: State files can be versioned using backends that support versioning, such as S3 with versioning enabled. Keeping a history of state versions allows you to roll back to a previous state if a bad apply corrupts or loses data. Terraform Cloud and Enterprise provide built-in state history and the ability to restore past versions.

nodes.name: Outputs
nodes.description: Terraform outputs expose selected values from a configuration or module, making them accessible to users or other modules. Defined in output blocks, typically in an `outputs.tf` file, they can reference resource attributes or other computed values. Outputs are displayed after apply operations, can be queried using terraform output commands, and are crucial for passing information between modules or to external systems.

nodes.name: Preconditions
nodes.description: Terraform preconditions are declarative checks within resource or data blocks that validate configuration or state before Terraform attempts to create or modify resources. They use condition arguments to specify logical tests and `error_message` arguments for custom failure notifications. Preconditions help catch misconfigurations early, enforce business rules, and ensure dependencies are met before resource operations.

resources.title: Using Precondition and Post-condition Blocks in Terraform

nodes.name: Variables
nodes.description: Terraform uses variables to make configurations more flexible and reusable. Variables can be declared in `.tf` files and assigned values through various methods, including default values, command-line flags, environment variables, or separate `.tfvars` files. They support multiple data types such as string, number, bool, list, and map. Variables can be referenced throughout the configuration using the `var` prefix. This system enables infrastructure as code to be more dynamic and adaptable to different environments or use cases.

resources.title: Learn How to Use Terraform Variable

nodes.name: Type Constraints
nodes.description: Terraform variable type constraints specify allowed data types for input variables. They include primitive types (string, number, bool), complex types (list, set, map, object), and any for unspecified types. Constraints can enforce specific structures, nested types, or value ranges. They're defined in the variable block's type argument, helping catch errors early and ensuring correct variable usage throughout configurations.

nodes.name: Variable Definition File
nodes.description: A Terraform `variables.tf` file centralizes input variable declarations for a module or configuration. It typically contains multiple variable blocks, each defining a single input variable with its name, type constraint, optional default value, and description. This file serves as a single reference point for all variables used in the configuration, enhancing readability and maintainability. While not mandatory, using `variables.tf` is a common practice to organize and document a module's expected inputs.

resources.title: You should be using tfvars vs variables in Terraform

nodes.name: Local Values
nodes.description: Local values can be understood as a name assigned to any expression to use it multiple times directly by the name in your terraform module. Local values are referred to as locals and can be declared using the `locals` block. Local values can be a literal constants, resource attributes, variables, or other local values. Local values are helpful to define expressions or values that you need to use multiple times in the module as it allows the value to be updated easily just by updating the local value. A local value can be accessed using the `local` argument like `local.<value_name>`.

nodes.name: Environment Variables
nodes.description: Environment variables can be used to customize various aspects of Terraform. You can set these variables to change the default behaviour of terraform such as increase verbosity, update log file path, set workspace, etc. Environment variables are optional and terraform does not need them by default.

nodes.name: Validation Rules
nodes.description: Validation rules can be used to specify custom validations to a variable. The motive of adding validation rules is to make the variable comply with the rules. The validation rules can be added using a `validation` block.

nodes.name: Format & Validate
nodes.description: Terraform provides built-in commands for formatting and validating configuration files before deployment. These commands help maintain consistent style and catch configuration errors early, before a plan or apply is attempted.

resources.title: Validate, format, lint, secure, and test Terraform IaC
Terraform Validate Command – Validate Configuration Locally

nodes.name: terraform fmt
nodes.description: `terraform fmt` rewrites Terraform configuration files to the canonical format and style defined by HashiCorp. It adjusts indentation, alignment, and spacing. Running it regularly, or as part of a pre-commit hook, keeps configurations consistent across a team.

resources.title: Using Terraform fmt Command to Format Your Terraform Code

nodes.name: terraform validate
nodes.description: The validate command helps you make sure your Terraform code is syntactically correct before you deploy. This helps you to prevent misconfiguration due to missing attributes or incorrect dependencies, saving time, improving efficiency, and reducing cost.

nodes.name: TFLint
nodes.description: TFLint is a Terraform linter that goes beyond the checks provided by `terraform validate`. It detects errors specific to provider APIs, such as invalid instance types or unsupported regions, and can enforce custom coding rules through plugins. It is commonly run in CI pipelines alongside `terraform validate`.

resources.title: What is TFLint and How to Lint Your Terraform Code

nodes.name: Best Practices for State
nodes.description: State should never be stored in version control, as it may contain sensitive values and is not designed for manual editing. Use a remote backend with locking and versioning enabled. Keep state files small by splitting large configurations into smaller modules with independent state, and run `terraform refresh` carefully as it overwrites state with live data.

resources.title: Managing Terraform State – Best Practices & Examples
Best Practices for Terraform State File Management
Managing Terraform State Files - What are your options?

nodes.name: count
nodes.description: The `count` meta-argument creates multiple instances of a resource or module from a single block. It accepts a whole number, and each instance is identified by an index starting at zero. Individual instances can be referenced using the `resource.name[index]` syntax.

resources.title: Conditional blocks in Terraform using count

nodes.name: for_each
nodes.description: The `for_each` meta-argument creates one instance of a resource or module for each item in a map or set of strings. Each instance is keyed by the map key or set value, making it easier to manage and reference individual items than with `count`. It is generally preferred over `count` when creating resources from a collection.

nodes.name: provider
nodes.description: The `provider` meta-argument assigns a specific provider configuration to a resource when multiple configurations of the same provider exist. This is common when managing resources across multiple regions or accounts within the same Terraform workspace. The value must match an alias defined in a `provider` block.

nodes.name: lifecycle
nodes.description: The `lifecycle` block inside a resource configures how Terraform handles creation, updates, and deletion of that resource. It supports arguments like `create_before_destroy`, `prevent_destroy`, `ignore_changes`, and `replace_triggered_by`. These settings give you fine-grained control over resource replacement behavior.

nodes.name: State
nodes.description: Terraform state is a file that records the current status of managed infrastructure. It maps resources in the configuration to real-world objects and stores attribute values returned by the provider after creation. State is used to compute diffs during planning and to track resource identity across operations.

nodes.name: Splitting State Files
nodes.description: Large Terraform configurations can be split into multiple state files by organizing resources into separate workspaces or root modules. This reduces the blast radius of plan and apply operations, speeds up plans, and makes it easier for teams to work independently on different parts of the infrastructure.

nodes.name: Import Existing Resources
nodes.description: `terraform import` brings existing infrastructure resources under Terraform management by adding them to the state file. After importing, the configuration must be written manually to match the imported resource. This is used when adopting Terraform in environments where resources were created outside of it.

resources.title: Terraform Import: What it is and how to use it
Exploring the Import Block in Terraform 1.5

nodes.name: State Locking
nodes.description: State locking prevents two Terraform operations from modifying state at the same time. When supported by the backend, Terraform acquires a lock before writing to state and releases it when the operation completes. If a lock is not released due to a crash or error, it can be manually removed with the `force-unlock` command.

nodes.name: Remote State
nodes.description: Remote state stores the Terraform state file in a shared, remote backend such as S3, Azure Blob Storage, or Terraform Cloud. This allows multiple team members to work with the same state and prevents conflicts from concurrent operations. Remote backends also support state locking to prevent simultaneous writes.

nodes.name: Published Modules Usage
nodes.description: Published modules are pre-built, versioned modules available on the Terraform Registry. They can be referenced directly in a `module` block using a registry source address and version constraint. Using published modules speeds up development by providing tested, maintained implementations of common infrastructure patterns.

nodes.name: Creating Local Modules
nodes.description: Local modules are directories containing Terraform configuration files that are referenced using a relative file path in a `module` block. They allow you to break a large configuration into smaller, self-contained units. Inputs are passed via variables and outputs are declared for the parent module to consume.

resources.title: Build and use a local module
How to create reusable infrastructure with Terraform modules

nodes.name: Inputs / Outputs
nodes.description: Modules accept input values through declared variables and expose results through declared outputs. The calling module passes values for each required variable and can reference the module's outputs using the `module.<name>.<output>` syntax. Well-defined inputs and outputs form the public interface of a module.

nodes.name: Modules Best Practices
nodes.description: Modules should be focused on a single concern and avoid hardcoding values that callers need to control. Always declare types for input variables and provide descriptions. Version-pin external modules and keep local modules small and composable. Avoid deeply nested module hierarchies, as they are harder to debug and maintain.

resources.title: Terraform Modules Guide: Best Practices & Examples
Best practices for modularizing a Terraform project | PlatformCon 2023

nodes.name: Inspect / Modify State
nodes.description: Terraform provides a set of commands for inspecting and modifying state directly. These are advanced operations used to fix drift, remove orphaned resources, or manually adjust state when normal plan and apply workflows are insufficient.

resources.title: How to Manage Terraform State: A Step-by-Step Guide

nodes.name: Output Syntax
nodes.description: An output block requires a `value` argument that specifies what to expose. Optional arguments include `description` for documentation, `sensitive` to redact the value, and `depends_on` to declare explicit dependencies. Outputs can expose any value, including resource attributes, local values, and variable values.

resources.title: Terraform Output Values : Complete Guide & Examples
Terraform: Output a field from a module

nodes.name: Sensitive Outputs
nodes.description: Marking an output as sensitive tells Terraform to redact its value from CLI output and logs. The value is still stored in state and can be accessed programmatically. This is commonly used for passwords, tokens, and other secrets that should not appear in plain text in terminal output.

resources.title: How to output sensitive data in Terraform

nodes.name: graph
nodes.description: `terraform graph` outputs a visual representation of the dependency graph for the current configuration or plan. The output is in DOT format, which can be rendered with tools like Graphviz. It is useful for understanding resource dependencies and diagnosing unexpected ordering issues.

resources.title: How to Generate Images with Terraform Graph Command

nodes.name: show
nodes.description: `terraform show` displays a human-readable representation of the current state or a saved plan file. It is useful for reviewing what Terraform currently knows about managed resources without running a full plan. Passing a plan file shows the exact changes that will be applied.

nodes.name: list
nodes.description: `terraform state list` prints the addresses of all resources tracked in the current state. It is a quick way to see what Terraform is managing and to find the exact resource address needed for other state subcommands. Addresses can be filtered by a resource type or module prefix.

nodes.name: output
nodes.description: `terraform output` displays the values of outputs defined in the configuration. Without arguments it shows all outputs; a specific output name can be passed to retrieve a single value. The `-json` flag returns output in machine-readable format, useful for scripting.

nodes.name: rm
nodes.description: `terraform state rm` removes one or more resources from the state file without destroying the actual infrastructure. This is used when you want Terraform to stop managing a resource, for example before importing it into a different workspace or before deleting it manually.

resources.title: Terraform State Rm: How to Remove a Resource From State File
How to remove resource from Terraform state file | terraform state rm example

nodes.name: mv
nodes.description: `terraform state mv` moves a resource address from one location to another within the state file. It is used when refactoring configurations, such as renaming a resource or moving it into a module, without triggering a destroy and recreate cycle.

nodes.name: -replace option in apply
nodes.description: The `-replace` flag on `terraform apply` forces Terraform to destroy and recreate a specific resource even if no configuration changes would normally trigger replacement. It is used to resolve issues with a corrupted or degraded resource that needs to be rebuilt. This replaces the older `taint` command.

resources.title: Terraform Taint, Untaint, Replace – How to Use It (Examples)
Terraform Taint Is Bad Actually - Use Replace Instead

nodes.name: state pull / push
nodes.description: `terraform state pull` downloads the current remote state and prints it to stdout. `terraform state push` uploads a local state file to the configured backend, overwriting the remote state. These commands are used for manual state recovery or migration and should be used with caution.

resources.title: Migrate Workspace State Using Terraform State Push / Pull

nodes.name: state replace-provider
nodes.description: `terraform state replace-provider` updates all resource entries in the state that reference one provider to reference a different provider. This is used when migrating resources to a forked or renamed provider without destroying and recreating them.

nodes.name: state force-unlock
nodes.description: `terraform state force-unlock` manually releases a state lock that was not properly released after an interrupted operation. It requires the lock ID, which is displayed in the error message shown when a lock conflict is detected. This command should only be used when you are certain no other Terraform operation is running.

nodes.name: Clean Up
nodes.description: Cleaning up Terraform-managed infrastructure means removing resources that are no longer needed. Terraform provides a command to destroy all resources in the current workspace, and understanding when and how to use it safely is an important part of the infrastructure lifecycle.

nodes.name: terraform destroy
nodes.description: `terraform destroy` removes all resources managed by the current configuration. It is the equivalent of running `terraform apply` with every resource marked for deletion. Like apply, it shows a plan and prompts for confirmation before proceeding. Individual resources can also be targeted with the `-target` flag.

nodes.name: Deployment
nodes.description: Deployment refers to the process of applying a configuration to create or update infrastructure. The typical workflow involves running `terraform plan` to preview changes and `terraform apply` to execute them. Understanding what happens during these steps is necessary for safe and predictable infrastructure management.

nodes.name: terraform plan
nodes.description: `terraform plan` computes the difference between the current state and the desired configuration and displays the actions Terraform would take. It does not make any changes to infrastructure. The plan can be saved to a file and passed to `terraform apply` to ensure the exact previewed changes are applied.

resources.title: Terraform plan command and how it works

nodes.name: terraform apply
nodes.description: `terraform apply` is the command used to implement the changes defined in your Terraform configuration files. It creates, updates, or deletes the specified infrastructure resources to match the desired state. Before making changes, it shows a plan similar to terraform plan and prompts for confirmation, unless the -auto-approve flag is used. Apply updates the state file to reflect the current infrastructure state, enabling Terraform to track and manage resources over time. It handles dependencies between resources, creating them in the correct order.

resources.title: Terraform Apply Command: Options, Examples and Best Practices

nodes.name: Modules
nodes.description: Modules are reusable packages of Terraform configuration that group related resources together. They allow you to abstract and share infrastructure patterns across projects and teams. Every Terraform configuration is technically a module; the directory you run Terraform from is called the root module.

nodes.name: Root vs Child Modules
nodes.description: The root module is the working directory where Terraform is invoked. Child modules are called from the root module or from other modules using a `module` block. Child modules can be local directories or remote sources such as the Terraform Registry or a Git repository.

resources.title: What is the difference between Terraform "Module" and "Child Module"

nodes.name: Provisioners
nodes.description: Provisioners run scripts or commands on local or remote machines as part of resource creation or destruction. They are a last resort for handling bootstrapping or configuration tasks that cannot be done through the provider API. HashiCorp recommends using purpose-built tools like cloud-init or Ansible instead where possible.

nodes.name: When to Use?
nodes.description: Provisioners are appropriate when no provider resource or data source can accomplish the required task and the action must happen at resource creation or destruction time. Common use cases include running initialization scripts on a new server or notifying an external system after a resource is created.
