They should be avoided when alternatives exist because they add complexity and are harder to test.

resources.title: Why You should Use Terraform Provisioners as a Final Option
Why Terraform Provisioners Are The Last Resort?

nodes.name: Creation / Destroy Time
nodes.description: Provisioners run either at creation time, after the resource is created, or at destroy time, before the resource is deleted. Creation-time provisioners bootstrap resources, while destroy-time provisioners handle cleanup tasks. If a creation-time provisioner fails, the resource is marked as tainted and will be destroyed and recreated on the next apply.

resources.title: How to: Terraform destroy time provisioners

nodes.name: file provisioner
nodes.description: The `file` provisioner copies files or directories from the machine running Terraform to a newly created remote resource. It requires a connection block specifying how to reach the remote machine, typically over SSH or WinRM. It is commonly used to upload configuration files or scripts before executing them.

nodes.name: local-exec provisioner
nodes.description: The `local-exec` provisioner runs a command on the machine executing Terraform, not on the remote resource. It is used for tasks like triggering an external API, running a local script, or writing data to a file. The command runs in a shell, and the working directory defaults to the Terraform configuration directory.

nodes.name: remote-exec provisioner
nodes.description: The `remote-exec` provisioner runs commands on the remote resource after it is created. It connects over SSH or WinRM and executes a list of inline commands or a script file. It is often used to install software or run configuration steps that cannot be handled by the provider.

nodes.name: Custom Provisioners
nodes.description: Custom provisioners can be implemented using external programs that follow the Terraform provisioner plugin protocol. They allow teams to integrate specialized tooling into the Terraform lifecycle without relying on the built-in provisioner types. Custom provisioners are rare and typically only needed for highly specific workflows.

resources.title: Terraform Provisioners - Why you should avoid them

nodes.name: Data Sources
nodes.description: Data sources allow Terraform to read information from external systems or from resources not managed in the current configuration. A `data` block queries a provider for information at plan time and makes the result available as a reference. Common uses include looking up AMI IDs, VPC details, or DNS zone information.

resources.title: Terraform Data Sources – How They Are Utilized

nodes.name: Template Files
nodes.description: Template files use the `templatefile` function to render a file with variable substitutions at plan time. The function takes a file path and a map of values and returns the rendered string. Template files are commonly used to generate user data scripts, configuration files, or policy documents from dynamic values.

nodes.name: CI / CD Integration
nodes.description: Integrating Terraform into a CI/CD pipeline automates infrastructure changes through the same review and deployment process used for application code. A typical pipeline runs `terraform fmt`, `terraform validate`, and `terraform plan` on pull requests, and `terraform apply` on merges to the main branch. Automation reduces human error and enforces a consistent workflow.

nodes.name: GitHub Actions
nodes.description: GitHub Actions can run Terraform commands as part of a workflow triggered by pull requests or pushes. Workflows are defined in YAML files and can use community actions from the GitHub Marketplace or call the Terraform CLI directly. Secrets for provider credentials are stored in the repository settings and injected as environment variables.

resources.title: Terraform with GitHub Actions : How to Manage & Scale

nodes.name: Circle CI
nodes.description: CircleCI can execute Terraform pipelines using orbs or custom job configurations. Jobs are defined in a `.circleci/config.yml` file and run in containers with the Terraform binary installed. It supports parallel jobs, caching, and approval steps that can be used to gate a `terraform apply` behind a manual review.

resources.title: Deploy Infrastructure with Terraform and CircleCI
How I deployed terraform resources with CircleCI

nodes.name: GitLab CI
nodes.description: GitLab CI runs Terraform pipelines using `.gitlab-ci.yml` configuration files. GitLab provides a native Terraform integration with merge request widgets that display plan output directly in the code review interface. The GitLab-managed Terraform state backend stores state securely within the GitLab instance.

resources.title: Infrastructure as Code with Terraform and GitLab
How to Implement GitLab CI/CD Pipeline with Terraform
Automate deploying to AWS using Terraform with GitLab CICD pipeline

nodes.name: Jenkins
nodes.description: Jenkins can orchestrate Terraform workflows using Pipeline scripts written in Groovy. The Terraform binary is installed on agents or provided via a tool configuration. Jenkins supports approval gates between plan and apply stages and integrates with secret management tools to supply provider credentials securely.

resources.title: Terraform with Jenkins – How to Manage Workflows
How to Use Terraform and Jenkins to Automate Infrastructure Setup

nodes.name: Workspaces
nodes.description: Workspaces allow multiple state files to exist for the same configuration, enabling the same code to manage separate environments such as development, staging, and production. The `terraform workspace` commands create, switch, and list workspaces. The current workspace name is available in expressions as `terraform.workspace`.

resources.title: Structuring Repositories for Terraform Workspaces - Hashicorp

nodes.name: Scaling Terraform
nodes.description: As infrastructure grows, Terraform configurations must be structured to remain manageable, performant, and safe for teams to use concurrently. Scaling strategies include splitting state, parallelizing operations, enforcing consistent deployment workflows, and managing version drift across modules and providers.

nodes.name: Version Management
nodes.description: Managing Terraform and provider versions across a team requires consistent tooling. `tfenv` is a popular version manager for Terraform that allows switching between installed versions based on a `.terraform-version` file. Pinning versions in `required_version` and `required_providers` blocks ensures everyone uses compatible releases.

resources.title: How to Use tfenv to Manage Multiple Terraform Versions

nodes.name: Splitting Large State
nodes.description: Large state files slow down plans and increase the risk of conflicts. Splitting infrastructure into smaller, independently managed configurations with their own state files reduces plan times and limits the impact of a failed apply. Resources in different state files communicate through remote state data sources or variable passing.

nodes.name: Parallelism
nodes.description: Terraform applies resource changes in parallel by default, up to a configurable limit controlled by the `-parallelism` flag. Increasing parallelism can speed up large deployments but may hit API rate limits. Lowering it can reduce throttling errors when working with providers that enforce strict rate limits.

resources.title: Considerations when setting the TFE_PARALLELISM environment variable

nodes.name: Deployment Workflow
nodes.description: A consistent deployment workflow defines how infrastructure changes move from development to production. Common patterns include environment promotion, where changes are applied to lower environments first, and GitOps, where the desired state is tracked in a Git repository and applied automatically. Enforcing a workflow reduces the risk of ad-hoc changes causing drift.

resources.title: Advanced Concepts and Faster Workflows in the Terraform Language

nodes.name: Terragrunt
nodes.description: Terragrunt is a thin wrapper around Terraform that adds support for keeping configurations DRY, managing dependencies between modules, and running commands across multiple modules at once. It uses `terragrunt.hcl` files to define module sources, variable inputs, and backend configuration. It is widely used in large multi-account or multi-environment Terraform setups.

resources.title: Terragrunt Tutorial: Examples and Use Cases

nodes.name: Infracost
nodes.description: Infracost is a cost estimation tool that integrates with Terraform to show the monthly cloud cost impact of planned infrastructure changes. It parses a Terraform plan and calculates costs based on provider pricing data. It can be added to CI pipelines to display cost breakdowns in pull request comments before changes are merged.

resources.title: Shifting FinOps Left: A live demo

nodes.name: Testing
nodes.description: Testing Terraform configurations verifies that infrastructure behaves as expected before and after deployment. Testing strategies range from static analysis and unit tests on modules to integration and end-to-end tests that provision real infrastructure. A layered testing approach catches different classes of problems at different stages of development.

nodes.name: Unit Testing
nodes.description: Unit tests for Terraform validate individual modules in isolation, checking that inputs produce the expected plan output without provisioning real resources. The native `terraform test` command introduced in Terraform 1.6 supports this by running configurations in a controlled context. Tools like Terratest can also be used for more complex scenarios.

nodes.name: Contract Testing
nodes.description: Contract testing verifies that the inputs and outputs of a module conform to a defined interface. It ensures that a module behaves predictably when called with specific values and that its outputs meet the expectations of callers. This is useful when modules are shared across multiple teams or projects.

resources.title: Contract Testing: An Introduction and Guide
Contract testing for microservices is a must!

nodes.name: Integration Testing
nodes.description: Integration tests provision real infrastructure and verify that resources are created correctly and work together as expected. They are slower and more expensive than unit tests but catch issues that static analysis cannot detect. Terratest is a popular Go-based framework for writing integration tests against live Terraform deployments.

resources.title: Learn Terraform - Integration and End-to-End Testing

nodes.name: End to End Testing
nodes.description: End-to-end tests validate an entire infrastructure stack by provisioning it, running checks against live endpoints or resources, and then tearing it down. These tests are the most comprehensive but also the slowest and most costly. They are typically run in a dedicated test environment and triggered on a schedule or before major releases.

resources.title: Getting Started: End to End Tests
End To End Testing On Terraform With Terratest

nodes.name: Testing Modules
nodes.description: Testing modules involves validating their logic, variable handling, and output values in isolation before they are used in a larger configuration. The `terraform test` command can apply a module with test-specific variable values and assert expected output values. Keeping modules testable means writing them with clear inputs and outputs and minimal side effects.

nodes.name: Security
nodes.description: Securing a Terraform workflow involves protecting secrets, enforcing policy on what infrastructure can be provisioned, and scanning configurations for misconfigurations before they reach production. A layered approach combines secret management, policy as code, and static analysis tools.

nodes.name: Secret Management
nodes.description: Secrets such as API keys, passwords, and certificates should never be stored in Terraform configuration files or committed to version control. Common approaches include injecting secrets via environment variables, using a secrets manager like HashiCorp Vault or AWS Secrets Manager as a data source, or using a backend that encrypts sensitive state values.

resources.title: Terraform Secrets - How to manage them
A comprehensive guide to managing secrets in your Terraform code

nodes.name: Compliance / Sentinel
nodes.description: Sentinel is a policy as code framework built into Terraform Cloud and Enterprise. It allows teams to define rules that restrict what infrastructure can be provisioned, enforce tagging standards, or require cost approval before applying. Policies are evaluated between the plan and apply phases, blocking deployments that violate defined rules.

nodes.name: Terrascan
nodes.description: Terrascan is an open-source static analysis tool that scans Terraform configurations for security and compliance violations before deployment. It checks against a library of built-in policies covering common cloud security standards and supports custom rules. It can be integrated into CI pipelines to fail builds that introduce insecure configurations.

nodes.name: Checkov
nodes.description: Checkov is a static analysis tool for infrastructure as code that scans Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, and other formats for security and compliance issues. It includes hundreds of built-in checks covering major cloud providers and supports custom policies written in Python or YAML. Scan results can be output as JUnit XML for integration with CI systems.

nodes.name: Trivy
nodes.description: Trivy is a security scanner that can analyze Terraform configurations for misconfigurations in addition to scanning container images and filesystems. It checks infrastructure code against a set of built-in rules and reports issues by severity. Trivy is easy to integrate into CI workflows and supports multiple output formats.

resources.title: How to secure Terraform code with Trivy

nodes.name: KICS
nodes.description: KICS (Keeping Infrastructure as Code Secure) is an open-source tool from Checkmarx that scans IaC files including Terraform for security vulnerabilities, compliance issues, and misconfigurations. It covers a broad set of cloud platforms and IaC formats and supports custom queries written in the Open Policy Agent Rego language.

nodes.name: HCP
nodes.description: HCP (HashiCorp Cloud Platform) is a managed cloud offering that hosts HashiCorp products including Terraform as a service. It provides a centralized place to manage Terraform runs, state, and policies without self-hosting the Terraform Enterprise platform.

nodes.name: What and when to use HCP?
nodes.description: HCP Terraform is appropriate when a team wants the benefits of Terraform Cloud, such as remote runs, state management, and policy enforcement, without managing infrastructure for it. It suits teams that are scaling beyond local Terraform workflows and need collaboration features, audit logs, and a managed backend. It is available in free and paid tiers.

nodes.name: Enterprise Features
nodes.description: HCP Terraform Enterprise features include audit logging, single sign-on, self-hosted deployment options, Sentinel policy enforcement, team and organization management, and private module registries. These features are aimed at large organizations that need governance controls and compliance capabilities beyond what the free tier provides.

resources.title: How does The Infrastructure Cloud work?

nodes.name: Authentication
nodes.description: HCP Terraform authenticates users and services through API tokens. User tokens are generated in the account settings and used for CLI access. Service account tokens are used in CI/CD pipelines. The `terraform login` command stores credentials locally for CLI use.

nodes.name: Workspaces
nodes.description: HCP Terraform workspaces are managed environments that store state, run history, and variable values for a specific configuration. Each workspace is linked to a version control repository or configured for CLI-driven runs. Variables and sensitive values are stored per workspace and injected into runs automatically.

resources.title: Organize your Terraform Cloud workspaces using Projects

nodes.name: VCS Integration
nodes.description: HCP Terraform integrates with version control systems including GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps. Linking a workspace to a VCS repository triggers speculative plans on pull requests and applies on merges to the configured branch. This brings infrastructure changes into the same code review workflow as application changes.

resources.title: Connecting VCS Providers to HCP Terraform

nodes.name: Run Tasks
nodes.description: Run Tasks are integrations that execute external services at specific points in the Terraform run lifecycle, such as after a plan or before an apply. They can be used to trigger security scans, cost checks, or custom validation logic. Run tasks return a pass or fail result that can block or allow the apply from proceeding.
